newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: OUB Bank 1st-half profits impress with 27 pct rise.
newsitem.headline: OUB Bank 1st-half profits impress with 27 pct rise.

text.p: Singapore's Overseas Union Bank Ltd (OUB) announced better than expected first half net profits on Friday and said earnings in the second six months of the year should be even better.
Net profit in the six months to June 30, 1997 rose 27.2 percent to Singapore $180.85 million (US$119.4 million) from S$142.15 million the year before, the bank said in a statement.
Consensus analyst forecasts had been for a rise of some 20 percent to around S$170 million.
"Clearly the numbers show we have done very well," OUB president and chief executive officer Peter Seah told a news conference.
"We believe this is a good story. This performance was achieved on the back of a 22.4 percent rise in loan portfolio for the group."
Seah said second-half results should be even better.
"I don't do crystal ball gazing, but I expect in terms of absolute quantum our second-half numbers to be higher than in the first-half," he said.
Seah said he had been asked at the 1996 full-year results news conference in March whether the bank's net profit for 1997 would reach Singapore $360 million.
"I said, 'maybe'," he said. "I think I have met that expectation." If the second-half matches the first six months, the full-year net would be around S$361.7 million.
Seah said the results were helped by strong contributions from outside Singapore, which accounted for around 35 percent of profits, up from 15-20 percent five years ago.
The biggest overseas contribution came from Malaysia, which made up 16 percent of profits. Post-tax profits at the bank's Malaysian subsidiary rose 37.2 percent to S$28.2 million.
Operations in Hong Kong and Australia also grew strongly.
Seah predicted the bank's profit contribution from outside Singapore would grow further in future and said he hoped it could reach 40 percent within the next two years.
"I foresee OUB evolving from a Singapore bank operating in the region into a regional bank based in Singapore," he said.
OUB's group interest income rose a strong 32.2 percent to S$1.2 billion, bringing its net group interest income to S$382.65 million, from S$322.12 million a year ago.
Other income rose 45.6 percent at group level to S$25.3 million, mainly arising from higher contributions from bullion and treasury operations, which Seah said had done very well.
Analysts greeted the results positively, saying the net result was comfortably in excess of expectations and put the bank on target for full-year results as forecast.
The latest edition of Edinburgh Financial Publishing's Estimate Directory suggests OUB's full-year net profit should come in some 19 percent higher at around S$371 million.
Keven Scully, head of research at Schroders in Singapore, said he saw no reason to change his 1997 forecast for OUB, which was slightly lower than the consensus at around S$358 million.
"I'm happy with these numbers. I think they are quite good," he told Reuters. "There is a margin expansion at the bank level, which is the only one we've seen from a local bank this year."
But Scully said he expected higher operating expenses in the second half of the year from more provisions for bad loans.

Seah said he expected some slowdown in loan growth in the second half of the year due to a developing slump in the local property market. But he said loans growth would still be in the "high-teens" to 20 percent range.
He said the bank was "quite comfortable" with its exposure in Thailand, which was bailed out by a US$16 billion rescue package put together, mainly by Asian nations, in Tokyo on Monday.
OUB proposed an unchanged interim dividend of five cents per share.
